subtype: Approach: asks several friends for suggestions [Action]
passage: The form for the Saturday junior league in the park had one empty box: TEAM NAME. It was due at the clubhouse by four o'clock. Gabriel grabbed a pencil and a paper bag from the kitchen. At the park he asked Owen, Ruby, Jack, Ella and Chloe, one by one, and wrote down every answer, even "The Fast Ones". Then he rang his cousin Nour. "The Leeds Lions," said Nour. "No, wait. The Wobbly Wickets." Gabriel read the whole list aloud on the bench. When he got to The Wobbly Wickets, Ruby snorted, Jack fell off the bench, and everyone laughed. Gabriel wrote it in the box and ran.

qa.q: How many friends did Gabriel ask at the park?
qa.a: Five: Owen, Ruby, Jack, Ella and Chloe, and then he rang his cousin Nour.

qa.q: How can you tell that Gabriel felt rushed?
qa.a: The form was due by four o'clock, he grabbed a paper bag to write on, and he ran as soon as the box was filled; he was in a hurry but excited.

qa.q: What else could Gabriel have done if nobody laughed at any name?
qa.a: He could let the team vote on their top two, so everyone still feels the name belongs to them.

qa.q: How might Nour feel when the team picks The Wobbly Wickets?
qa.a: Nour would probably feel proud and amused that the joke name won 😊

grounding: A boy collects team-name ideas from five friends and a cousin, writes them all down and picks the one that made everyone laugh.

subtype: Approach: asks several friends for suggestions [Action]
passage: At the sports club's summer camp, the coach said every team needed a name before the T-shirts went to print on Friday. Kiran's team stared at each other. Kiran took the marker and went to the whiteboard. "Everyone gives one idea. I write it, no matter what." Five teammates shouted names: Thunder, Blue Stars, Sixers, Tiger Team, Boundary Kings. Then Kiran's cousin Madhav, who was helping with the kit, said, "Samosa Strikers." Kiran wrote that too. He read the list out slowly. At Samosa Strikers, the whole team burst out laughing, and even the coach grinned. Kiran circled it twice.

qa.q: What were the five names the teammates shouted?
qa.a: Thunder, Blue Stars, Sixers, Tiger Team and Boundary Kings.

qa.q: Why did Kiran promise to write every idea 'no matter what'?
qa.a: He wanted everyone to feel included and not embarrassed to share, which is why even the silly idea made the list.

qa.q: What could Kiran try if two names got equal laughs?
qa.a: He could ask the team to raise hands for one of the two, so the choice stays fair.

qa.q: How does Madhav see his joke being chosen?
qa.a: Madhav probably feels delighted and a bit surprised that his silly suggestion became the team's real name.

grounding: A boy asks five teammates and his cousin for team names, lists them all and circles the one that made everyone laugh.

subtype: Approach: polls a class group for options [Action]
passage: Looking back, the farewell gift for Sen Sir was the first time I organised anything properly. I'm Vinita, and I was class rep that year. On the Monday, I posted in our class group: "Ideas for Sen Sir's farewell gift? Anything goes. Reply by Wednesday night." By Wednesday there were thirty replies, some serious, some just stickers. Omkar suggested a chess set because Sir played in the staffroom. Others wanted a plant, a photo album, a pen. I copied every idea into my notebook and grouped them: things for his hobbies, things with memories, useful things. Memories had the most, fourteen. So we made an album with a message from each of us. When Sir opened it, he went very quiet, then smiled.

qa.q: How many replies did Vinita get by Wednesday?
qa.a: By Wednesday there were thirty replies.

qa.q: What was Vinita feeling when Sen Sir went quiet and then smiled?
qa.a: Vinita likely felt relieved and proud that the idea chosen from the class's replies had touched Sen Sir.

qa.q: What else could Vinita have done after sorting the ideas?
qa.a: Vinita could post the three themes back to the class for a quick vote, so everyone sees their idea counted.

qa.q: How might Omkar feel when the album was chosen over his chess set?
qa.a: Omkar might feel a small pang, but since his idea was counted and memories clearly won, he would likely still feel part of it.

grounding: A student asks the class group for farewell gift ideas, gathers thirty replies and sorts them into themes.

subtype: Approach: polls a class group for options [Action]
passage:
Class teacher's note, 9C, Friday

This week Sharmila took on the Annual Day gift for our retiring librarian. I watched her handle it. She posted one question in the class group on Monday: "One idea each, please, by Thursday." She did not argue with anyone. By Thursday she had thirty replies. Ira helped her copy them onto chart paper in the free period, and together they grouped them: books, garden things, handmade items, experiences. Handmade had the most. Sharmila came to me with the four groups and a clear recommendation. I suggested she check the budget with the class treasurer and let the class vote between the top two groups on Monday. She looked pleased and went off to draft the poll.

qa.q: By when did Sharmila ask for ideas?
qa.a: By Thursday, one idea each.

qa.q: How did Sharmila seem to feel when the class teacher gave the suggestion?
qa.a: She looked pleased, suggesting she felt encouraged that her work was taken seriously.

qa.q: What could Sharmila do if the vote ended in a tie?
qa.a: She could combine the two themes, such as a handmade card with a book, or ask the librarian's closest colleague which would mean more.

qa.q: How might Ira see working on the chart paper?
qa.a: Ira likely felt useful and included, sharing the work of making sense of thirty replies.

grounding: A student polls the class group for gift ideas, collects thirty replies and sorts them into themes.

subtype: Approach: collects suggestions from a wide community and looks for repeated patterns [Thinking]
passage: I still remember the night we read those replies. I'm Santosh, and in second year I ran the welcome committee. We posted a simple question on the college forum: "Seniors, what confused you most in your first week?" More than eighty people answered. Madhav and I sat in the canteen with the list. At first it was just noise: Wi-Fi, mess timings, lost ID cards. Then I started tallying. I said to Madhav, "Wait. Curfew, guest rules, laundry days, getting a late pass. These are all the same thing. It's hostel rules." We counted: thirty-one replies were about hostel rules. Nobody had said "hostel rules" in those words; they were hiding in different complaints. So that year our orientation opened with a hostel-rules session, not the campus tour.

qa.q: How many replies were about hostel rules?
qa.a: Thirty-one replies were about hostel rules.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel when the pattern appeared?
qa.a: Santosh felt a jolt of excitement and surprise, seeing that curfew, guest rules, laundry days and late passes were all one problem.

qa.q: What would you change first if you were running the next orientation?
qa.a: Check with this year's freshers after the hostel-rules session whether it helped, and post the question again to spot any new pattern.

qa.q: How might the freshers experience orientation after this change?
qa.a: Freshers would feel less lost in their first week, since their biggest confusion is answered on day one.

grounding: A student club collects many replies about orientation and, by tallying, sees that confusion about hostel rules keeps repeating.

subtype: Approach: collects suggestions from a wide community and looks for repeated patterns [Thinking]
passage:
Faculty adviser's note: Student Welfare Club, September

Sudha and Vandana asked for my time today to show what they found. The club had asked the online student community one question: what problems did you face in orientation? They got about sixty answers. Sudha had printed them and highlighted by colour. She explained her thinking aloud: "At first I sorted by topic and got twelve piles. Then I noticed the same worry under different names: nobody knew when the hostel gates close, whether visitors are allowed, who to ask for a late entry. That's one confusion, not twelve." Vandana added that the replies came from four different hostels. I suggested they meet the chief warden this week. They left with an appointment.

qa.q: How many answers did the club get?
qa.a: About sixty answers.

qa.q: What does Sudha's explanation suggest about how she felt once she spotted the pattern?
qa.a: She seems confident and relieved: twelve confusing piles turned into one clear problem about hostel rules.

qa.q: What could Sudha and Vandana do next, besides meeting the chief warden?
qa.a: They could draft a one-page hostel rules guide for freshers and share it back with the community to check it answers the confusion.

qa.q: How might the chief warden see the students' findings?
qa.a: The warden may feel informed and willing to act, since the evidence comes from four hostels, not one complaint.

grounding: A student club gathers replies from the wider community and reasons aloud about the repeated confusion around hostel rules.

subtype: Approach: takes the most upvoted idea without checking it fits [Pitfall]
passage: You want to know my biggest mistake? Okay. I'm Himani, and I make scented candles. Last Diwali season I wanted a new fragrance, so I posted a poll on my page: sandalwood, coffee, or rose. Coffee won by a mile, almost four hundred votes. I was thrilled. I ordered coffee oil in bulk and poured two hundred candles. Then they just... sat there. Darshan, who runs the gift shop that stocks me, said, "Your buyers are aunties buying gifts for pujas. They want sandalwood." I went back to the poll. Most voters were other small business owners and college friends. Nice people, but not my buyers. I'd counted votes without asking whose votes they were. I still have coffee candles in my cupboard.

qa.q: How many candles did Himani pour with coffee oil?
qa.a: Two hundred candles.

qa.q: How did Himani feel when the coffee candles didn't sell?
qa.a: Himani went from thrilled to embarrassed and deflated, and still keeps the leftovers as a reminder.

qa.q: What would you advise Himani to do before the next launch?
qa.a: Check who is voting and ask actual buyers, like the customers at Darshan's shop, then make a small trial batch first.

qa.q: How did the situation look from Darshan's side?
qa.a: Darshan could see the gift shop's customers wanted sandalwood, and probably felt awkward having unsold stock on the shelf.

grounding: A small business owner adopts the top choice from a social media poll, but the voters are not the business's buyers and the candles do not sell.

subtype: Approach: takes the most upvoted idea without checking it fits [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Rashmi, and I live across the landing from Sangeeta, who runs a lunchbox service for the offices near the station. Last month she asked her followers online to pick a new Friday dish. I saw the poll: pasta bowl won easily. On Friday morning her kitchen smelled of cheese and garlic instead of the usual dal. She packed forty boxes. That evening she came back up the stairs carrying most of them. I heard her on the phone, sounding flat: "They asked for rajma-chawal. Of course they did." For the next few days she was quieter than usual, and the Friday pasta vanished from her menu. I don't know exactly what she felt. But I noticed she started chatting with her delivery boy about what customers said.

qa.q: How many boxes did Sangeeta pack on Friday?
qa.a: She packed forty boxes.

qa.q: What does Sangeeta's flat voice on the phone suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt disappointed and maybe a bit foolish that her followers' choice didn't match what her office customers wanted.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: The voters weren't her lunch customers; she could ask her office buyers directly, or send a few trial pasta boxes before cooking forty.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta's regular customers have felt that Friday?
qa.a: They were probably puzzled or let down to get pasta when they wanted home-style food like rajma-chawal.

grounding: An observer describes a small business owner adopting a poll's top choice from people who are not her customers, and the product failing.

subtype: Approach: weighs the answers by who gave them and tests the top few [Revision]
passage:
"Two hundred replies, Aditi. Just make the chilli-garlic, it got the most."
"Tushar, last time I did that we were stuck with jars nobody bought."
"So what, then?"
"Look." She turned the laptop. "I marked who actually ordered from us this year. Only sixty of these are real customers."
"And what do those sixty want?"
"Lemon-ginger and mixed-veg. Chilli-garlic came fourth."
"So we make lemon-ginger?"
"We make both, small. Twenty jars each, at the Sunday stall."
Sunday evening:
"Lemon-ginger gone by noon. Mixed-veg, six left."
"Okay," Aditi said, closing the ledger. "Lemon-ginger stays on the menu. Mixed-veg we try once more with a smaller jar."
Tushar laughed. "You're getting strict with your own polls."
"I've learnt which votes to count 🙂"

qa.q: How many of the two hundred replies came from real customers?
qa.a: Only sixty of these are real customers.

qa.q: Why was Aditi reluctant to just make the chilli-garlic pickle?
qa.a: She was wary because the last time she followed the top vote, they were stuck with jars nobody bought.

qa.q: What makes Aditi's approach this time better than simply going with the top vote?
qa.a: She filtered for real customers and tested two options in small batches, so the market, not the loudest voices, decided.

qa.a: He seems amused and impressed, teasing that she is getting strict with her own polls.

subtype: Approach: weighs the answers by who gave them and tests the top few [Revision]
passage: When I think about my second year of soap-making, I think about a spreadsheet. I'm Aparna. That spring I asked for scent ideas online and got over a hundred answers. The year before, I'd simply made the favourite, and a whole shelf of it went unsold. This time I did something different. I filtered the list down to people who had actually bought from me. Only thirty-five were left. Among them, neem-tulsi and orange-clove kept coming up. My friend Akash helped me cut small test bars, thirty of each, for the weekend market. By Sunday the orange-clove was gone and neem-tulsi had twelve left. I kept orange-clove. It's still my best-seller, and I still check who is answering before I count a vote.

qa.q: How many people were left after Aparna filtered the list?
qa.a: Only thirty-five were left.

qa.q: How did Aparna feel about the previous year's approach?
qa.a: Aparna felt uneasy and wary after a whole shelf of the favourite went unsold, which is why the approach changed.

qa.a: Akash gets to see the result quickly and may feel satisfied that the test bars led to a clear answer.

grounding: The soap-maker narrows suggestions to real customers, tests two in small batches and keeps the one buyers pick.

subtype: Approach: works out what each side wants and finds a swap [Thinking]
passage: At the colony library, there was only one reserved table with a lamp, and Amandeep and her brother Jasraj both wanted it. "I need it after school," Jasraj said. "My model volcano won't fit on the bed." Amandeep folded her arms. Then she stopped. "Wait. When do you actually need it?" "Four to six. Then I have football." Amandeep counted on her fingers. "I don't care about afternoons. I need it after dinner, because that's when I read for my test. So you take four to six, and I take seven to nine." Jasraj blinked. "That's it?" "We both want different times. We were fighting for nothing." The librarian wrote both names on the booking card.

qa.q: When does Jasraj need the table?
qa.a: Four to six, then he has football.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling when she folded her arms, and what changed?
qa.a: At first she felt annoyed and ready to fight, but she calmed down once she worked out that they wanted different times.

qa.q: What small step helped them solve it?
qa.a: Asking "When do you actually need it?" made it clear the two wants didn't clash, so a split was easy.

qa.q: How does Jasraj see Amandeep's solution?
qa.a: He is surprised and relieved; he expected a fight and instead got the hours he needed.

grounding: Two siblings want the same study table; the girl needs it after dinner, the boy in the afternoon, so they split the hours.

subtype: Approach: works out what each side wants and finds a swap [Thinking]
passage: I'm Nazia, the cousin who lived with them that year, and I watched this one from the sofa. Tanvir and Tanuja both wanted the big study table in the hall, the only one with enough space. Every afternoon there was shouting. One Sunday, Tanuja took a paper and drew two columns. "What do you want the table for, and when?" she asked Tanvir. He grumbled: "Afternoons. I do my drawings when there's light." She wrote it down. "I study best after dinner, when it's quiet." She looked at the paper for a while. "So afternoons are yours, nights are mine." Tanvir squinted at it, then nodded. The shouting stopped. I can't say what each of them really felt, but the table had two neat timetables taped on it by Monday.

qa.a: Two columns.

qa.a: He is doubtful at first, squinting, but then relieved, since the afternoons with good light are his.

grounding: An observer watches siblings work out who needs the table when, then agree on split hours.

subtype: Approach: separates a demand from the interest behind it [Thinking]
passage:
"Ammi, the birthday dinner at Kabeer's goes on till ten-thirty. Can I stay?"
"Asif, no. Home by eight."
"Everyone's staying!"
"I said eight."
Asif went to his room and sat on the bed. Why eight? It's not the dinner she minds. He went back out. "Ammi, what's the worry, exactly?"
She put down the dishcloth. "That last bus. Empty roads. You alone."
"So it's the travel, not the party."
"It's the travel."
"What if my cousin Ayesha picks me up? She finishes work at ten near there."
Ammi looked at him for a long moment. "If Ayesha says yes, and you're at the gate when she comes."
"I'll call her now."
Ayesha texted back in a minute: "Fine, 10:30 sharp."

qa.q: What time did Ammi first say Asif should be home?
qa.a: Home by eight.

qa.q: What was Ammi really worried about?
qa.a: Ammi was anxious about the travel: the last bus, empty roads and Asif alone, not the party itself.

qa.q: Which approach worked for Asif, and why?
qa.a: Asking what the worry was, then solving that worry with a safe pickup; arguing "everyone's staying" had gotten him nowhere.

qa.q: If you were Ayesha, what would you want from Asif?
qa.a: You'd want him to be at the gate at 10:30 sharp, so the favour stays easy and trust grows.

grounding: A teenager sees that his mother's worry is safe travel, not the late stay, and offers to be picked up by his cousin.

subtype: Approach: separates a demand from the interest behind it [Thinking]
passage: The project night at Vasudha's house was the first time I really thought about why my parents said no. I'm Yusuf. We had a model to finish and then a film, which meant leaving around eleven. Abbu said, "Beta, no. Back by nine." I nearly argued, the way I always did. Instead I lay on my bed and thought: what is he actually scared of? It wasn't Vasudha, he knew her family. It wasn't the film. It was the auto ride back through the market after dark. So I went to him and said, "What if my cousin brings me back on his bike? He works late near there anyway." Abbu thought about it. "Call him first, then ask me again." My cousin said yes. I stayed till eleven.

qa.q: What time did Abbu first ask Yusuf to be back?
qa.a: Back by nine.

qa.q: What did Yusuf work out about Abbu's feelings?
qa.a: Yusuf realised Abbu was scared about the auto ride back through the market after dark, not about Vasudha or the film.

qa.q: What would you advise a friend who always argues with a parent's 'no'?
qa.a: First ask or think about what the real worry is, then offer a plan that answers it, like a trusted ride home.

qa.q: How might Abbu see Yusuf's offer?
qa.a: Abbu likely felt reassured and a little impressed that his son thought about his fear instead of just arguing.

grounding: A teenager realises his parent's worry is the ride home and offers to be picked up by his cousin.

subtype: Approach: prepares options and a fallback before talking [Action]
passage: By second year, I knew the chore talk with my flatmates could go badly. The first time, I'd just said, "This is unfair," and we spent an hour shouting about dishes. I'm Arohi, by the way. So this time, the night before, I wrote down three rota options: one person per week for everything; kitchen, bathroom and bins rotating; or each person keeping one job for a month. I also decided my limit: I could live with any plan, as long as the bathroom wasn't mine two months running. When Zeenat and I sat down with our third flatmate, I laid the paper on the table. Zeenat liked the rotating one. I agreed straight away. The whole talk took fifteen minutes and nobody raised their voice.

qa.q: How many rota options did Arohi write down?
qa.a: Three rota options.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel going into the talk this time?
qa.a: Arohi felt calm and prepared, knowing the options and the one limit that mattered.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who dreads a chore talk?
qa.a: Write a few options in advance and decide what you can accept, so you can listen instead of defending.

qa.q: How might Zeenat see the talk this time compared with the first?
qa.a: Zeenat probably felt more relaxed and heard, getting to pick a plan instead of being accused.

grounding: A student lists rota options before talking to flatmates and knows what is acceptable, so the talk stays calm.

subtype: Approach: prepares options and a fallback before talking [Action]
passage:
Hostel warden's note, Block C, room 214

The three girls in 214 have argued about cleaning since August. Today I watched Irawati bring it up in the common room. She came with a sheet listing three possible rotas: by day, by week, and by task. She told me beforehand that she could accept any of them, except taking the water-can refills alone every day, because of her early lab. Payal wanted weekly turns. Irawati said, "That works for me if refills rotate daily." Their third roommate agreed. The discussion was calm and took under twenty minutes. I asked them to pin the rota on the door and to come back to me in two weeks if it isn't working.

qa.a: By day, by week, and by task.

qa.q: What could the roommates do if the rota stops working?

qa.q: How might Payal have experienced the talk?
qa.a: Payal likely felt heard, since her weekly idea was accepted with only a small change about refills.

grounding: A student prepares rota options and knows her limit before talking with roommates, and the talk is calm.

subtype: Approach: treats it as winner takes all and damages the relationship [Pitfall]
passage: At the small cooperative dairy outside Nashik, there was one delivery van for two routes. Eshaan wanted it every morning for the town route, where the big orders were. But over the next weeks, Sahil stopped helping him load crates. The storeman became slow with Eshaan's slips. When the van broke down in November and Eshaan asked Sahil to lend his motorbike for one urgent drop, Sahil shook his head. "Ask the secretary," he said. Eshaan stood by the milk cans, realising the win had cost him every favour he used to get free.

qa.q: Which days did Sahil need the van?
qa.a: On Tuesdays, for the villages.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling as he stood by the milk cans?
qa.a: Eshaan felt stunned and regretful, realising his win had cost him the goodwill of the people around him.

qa.a: Apologise to Sahil and offer to give up the van on Tuesdays, rebuilding trust before asking for anything else.

qa.q: How does Sahil see Eshaan after the meeting?
qa.a: Sahil sees him as someone who takes everything, so he feels no pull to help when Eshaan is in trouble.

grounding: A team member wins the argument over the van, but colleagues stop cooperating and later refuse him a favour.

subtype: Approach: asks what the other side needs and reshapes the deal [Revision]
passage: Elizabeth had been going round in circles with Madhuri for a week. Madhuri's flower stall in the Dadar market supplied the event company Elizabeth worked for, and Elizabeth needed a lower price for three weddings in December. Madhuri wouldn't budge. On Thursday, standing between buckets of marigolds, Elizabeth stopped pushing. "Madhuri-tai, tell me honestly. What matters most to you right now?" Madhuri wiped her hands. "Payment. Your company pays after forty-five days. I buy flowers in cash every morning." Elizabeth thought for a moment. "If I get you paid within a week of each wedding, can you do the price we talked about?" Madhuri looked at her a long time. "Within a week, in writing, then yes." Elizabeth rang her accounts team from the stall.

qa.q: How long did the company take to pay Madhuri before?
qa.a: After forty-five days.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel when she stopped pushing and asked her question?
qa.a: She was probably frustrated after a week of circling, and a little hopeful that asking Madhuri's real need could open things up.

qa.q: Which approach worked better than pushing on price, and why?
qa.a: Asking what mattered most; once Elizabeth knew Madhuri needed quick payment, she could offer that in exchange for the lower price.

qa.q: What is it like for Madhuri to be asked that question?
qa.a: Madhuri probably feels respected and relieved, since her cash problem is finally being heard.

grounding: After a stalemate, she asks the vendor what matters most, learns it is quick payment, and trades earlier payment for a lower price.

subtype: Approach: asks what the other side needs and reshapes the deal [Revision]

"Hansa-ji, we've been at this for twenty minutes."

qa.a: Afreen could offer a larger order spread over months, or a fixed payment date, whichever Hansa values more.

qa.q: How might Hansa's printer be affected by the deal?
qa.a: The printer is likely to get paid on time more easily, since Hansa no longer waits two months for her money.

grounding: After a stalemate, the bakery owner asks the supplier what matters most, learns it is payment speed, and trades earlier payment for a lower price.
